summary: The United Arab Emirates is made up of seven emirates, founded in 1971, and is known for its oil wealth, the skyscrapers of Dubai and its international aviation hub; foreigners make up about 90 percent of the population.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Soon after Islam arose in the Arabian Peninsula in the 7th century, the tribes of Oman and of what is now the UAE accepted Islam; the Emirati citizens are almost all Muslims, mainly Sunni of the Maliki and Hanbali schools, with a minority of Shia. When the country was founded in 1971 the constitution made Islam the state religion; however, because foreign residents make up nearly 90 percent of the total population, Muslims account for only about three quarters of all residents.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christians are almost all foreign workers, mainly from the Philippines, the Indian state of Kerala, Europe and America, and Lebanon. After oil exports began in the 1960s, the rulers of the various emirates successively granted land for building churches to attract foreign professionals; for example, the first Catholic church in Abu Dhabi was completed in 1965, and when Pope Francis visited Abu Dhabi in 2019 it was the first time a pope had set foot on the Arabian Peninsula.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hindus are the large numbers of migrant workers and merchants from India. Indian merchants were already doing business in Dubai during the British protection period of the 19th century, and Dubai had a Hindu temple by 1958; after the oil boom of the 1970s Indian immigration surged, and the completion in 2024 of the large stone Hindu temple (BAPS temple) in Abu Dhabi reflects the size of this community.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhists are mainly foreign workers and professionals from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Nepal and East Asia, who mostly meet in private venues or temples in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. Because most of them are short-term contract workers, the community is highly fluid, and its share is around 2 percent.

religion.background: Before Islam arrived in the 7th century, the inhabitants of southeastern Arabia followed polytheistic beliefs, and there were also a few Christian settlements; for example, the remains of a monastery of the 7th and 8th centuries have been found on Sir Bani Yas Island. After Islamization the local tribes were mainly Sunni, and Islam was the basis of tribal society and law. When the UAE was founded in 1971, the constitution made Islam the state religion and Islamic law the main source of legislation. The oil economy brought a large foreign population, making the UAE a country of highly diverse religious composition, and the government also uses 'tolerance' as its national image, even establishing a Ministry of Tolerance in 2016.

language.official: Arabic is the official language, and English is widely used in business and daily communication.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic is the official language of the UAE and the mother tongue of its citizens, and the local spoken form is Gulf Arabic. However, Emirati citizens make up only about one tenth of the national population, and together with Arab immigrants from Egypt, Lebanon, Syria and elsewhere, only about two tenths of people have Arabic as a mother tongue; the government and courts use Modern Standard Arabic, while everyday business mostly uses English.

ranking.name: Malayalam
ranking.description: Malayalam is the language of the Indian state of Kerala. The Kerala coast has had spice trade with the Arabian Peninsula since ancient times, and after the oil boom of the 1970s large numbers of Keralites went to the Gulf states to work in construction, commerce and medicine, making Malayalam one of the largest immigrant languages in the UAE.

ranking.name: Urdu
ranking.description: Urdu is the national language of Pakistan and the mother tongue of many Indian Muslims. Since the 1970s Pakistanis have gone to the UAE in large numbers to work in construction, transport and services, and Urdu and the closely related Hindi, spread by Bollywood films, have become common languages of communication among migrant workers.

ranking.name: Tagalog
ranking.description: Tagalog (Filipino) is spoken by the several hundred thousand Filipinos working in the UAE. Since the 1970s the Philippines has promoted an overseas worker policy, and large numbers of nurses, domestic workers and service staff have gone to the Gulf; Tagalog is often heard in Dubai's shopping malls and restaurants.

language.history: The inhabitants of the UAE area have used Arabic since Islamization, and the local dialect is Gulf Arabic, close to the dialects of Oman, Qatar and Bahrain. From the 19th century Britain signed treaties with local sheikhs, forming the protection system of the 'Trucial States', and English began to appear in administration and trade. After oil exports began in the 1960s, large numbers of South Asian, Southeast Asian and Western immigrants poured in, and by the 21st century the foreign population made up nearly 90 percent, so English became the common language among different groups. In recent years the government has promoted Arabic-language education and signage policies in order to prevent the citizens' mother tongue from being marginalized in an English-speaking environment.

ranking.name: Machboos
ranking.description: Chicken, lamb or fish is stewed together with long-grain rice, with dried lime, saffron, cinnamon and baharat spice blend added; the rice soaks up the meat juices and is richly fragrant.
ranking.history: Machboos is the representative rice dish of the Gulf region; the rice used is not grown locally but was imported from India through long-standing Indian Ocean trade, and the spices also come from India and Persia, so it is often regarded as sharing an origin with Indian biryani. Dried lime (loomi) is a specialty of Oman and the Persian Gulf coast. Before the oil era, fishermen and pearl divers made machboos with fish, and today it is the main dish of Emirati family Friday lunches and wedding banquets.

ranking.name: Harees
ranking.description: Wheat grains and meat (mostly chicken or lamb) are stewed for a long time and then repeatedly beaten into a thick porridge with a smooth texture, and it is served with ghee poured over.
ranking.history: Harees is one of the oldest dishes of the Arabian Peninsula, and it is already recorded in Arabic cookbooks of 10th-century Baghdad. It is especially common at the breaking of the fast during Ramadan and at Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, and even wealthy households cook large pots of harees to share with neighbors and the poor. It is made by stewing the wheat and meat for several hours and beating it with a wooden pestle; the laborious process makes it a symbol of festivals and the spirit of sharing, and it is also a traditional dish often seen at Emirati wedding banquets.

ranking.name: Luqaimat
ranking.description: Spoonfuls of fermented batter are dropped into oil in small balls and fried, then drizzled with date syrup and sprinkled with sesame seeds; they are crisp outside and soft inside, with the aroma of saffron and cardamom.
ranking.history: Luqaimat means 'small bites', and it belongs to the same ancient class of desserts as Greek honey-fried dough balls and Indian fried sweet balls; similar 'luqmat al-qadi' already appears in Arabic cookbooks of 13th-century Baghdad. The date is the most important crop of the Arabian Peninsula, and flavoring with date syrup is precisely the local specialty. It is most popular at the breaking of the fast during Ramadan and is also a must-have snack for entertaining guests at weddings and festivals.

ranking.name: Balaleet
ranking.description: Thin vermicelli noodles (fine Italian-style pasta threads) are stir-fried with sugar, saffron, rose water and cardamom and topped with a layer of omelet, blending sweet and savory.
ranking.history: Balaleet is a traditional breakfast of the Gulf region, eaten especially on the mornings of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. The combination of vermicelli, saffron and rose water reflects the trade between the Persian Gulf and Persia and India, while the way of eating sweet noodles with a salty egg is a specialty of the UAE, Bahrain and elsewhere. In the past it was a luxurious breakfast for which sugar and spices were used only at festivals, and today it is still common in homes and traditional restaurants.

ranking.name: Thareed
ranking.description: Flatbread is torn up and laid at the bottom of a plate, and a thick stew of lamb or chicken with vegetables such as potato and pumpkin is poured over it, and it is eaten after the bread has soaked up the broth.
ranking.history: Thareed is one of the oldest dishes of the Arab world, and Islamic tradition records that the Prophet Muhammad loved this dish, so it holds a special place in Muslim society. The traditional method uses the local flatbread (regag), combining leftover bread with meat broth, which also reflects the desert habit of treasuring food. In the UAE it is a common dish for the evening meal that breaks the fast during Ramadan.
